— The nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening has highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure that has had several disruptive failures in recent months."},{"_id":"TKCGDRBHAFF3VL6UHVDK7AYQKY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Officials called the rare ground stop after outdated communications lines became overloaded and began to fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin."},{"_id":"FZOF62F64NGKLEH4ZJA2WSEY5Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The breakdown occurred less than two months after a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush International Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line."},{"_id":"KHKDJEBNPBEXRJ2IHKVQV2HNFY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the FAA has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. The FAA has yet to identify precisely what caused communication lines to falter."},{"_id":"JIGMDC7ICJEYBKHOIXOMNM5XIA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Associated Press reported that Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said Saturday that the U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of today. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”"},{"_id":"YNB7FWHTTNH4HCZI6C7VXIL2XQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said."},{"_id":"DFIKVJG35JEFJGLK45KPK2R74A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause."},{"_id":"QPKYH6LC3FG6NM6YFT3OFZA2PI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment,” Duffy said."},{"_id":"5NEDTLYXOZBLLNUDK2NKRHVJ7E","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the successive episodes of such problems have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that continue to hamper air traffic controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after concerted efforts to make improvements. And they raised questions about whether the federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems and redundancies to prevent disruptive or even catastrophic failures."},{"_id":"BNMOUXOZTJD3RP2MRJYRKHKNXM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"For decades, air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks, and alphabetical keyboards so old that the FAA has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to help pay for upgrades, after a series of outages in air traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, caused alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities."},{"_id":"LSZ4PGSALZDSBO7T45UN6CBGQY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecoms contractor tasked to manage the system upgrades, boasted on its website that it had converted about 70% of the copper line to fiber optic cable; last week, the FAA announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks."},{"_id":"Q6KS2XJEOFGV7FBDZETY33EUCI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the disruptions in recent weeks showed that those upgrades had serious vulnerabilities themselves."},{"_id":"E6BY4EP4HZBC5BTBVRQ2HDUTHQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered — to their surprise — had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later."},{"_id":"LSIQDWL3BZGHNFAPIYBN65E7AY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A similar incident occurred in October at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina, when a contractor working on plumbing accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. Just one day after that, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush International Airport, when yet another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line."},{"_id":"4Y5DCM5WBBFX7KO6TLENUQAHW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The fiber line upgrades themselves, Bedford, the FAA administrator, told reporters at the time, were not enough to save the system from failure."},{"_id":"ZQ54KCD6YZE4JPTQDGUFG2HSY4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Ideally, the FAA wanted to put data into cloud services, he told reporters then, so that “when you have a fiber cut, you have multiple pathways of backup.”"},{"_id":"FNIXXMAUH5A7BIE6SLYLM4ILQQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today we have physical fiber and when it’s cut, there’s one redundancy, and when we lose that, there’s no more redundancy,” he added."},{"_id":"LKQ6CSVCTZDJZL6OIZMOBBATOQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Friday’s national ground stop revealed that the lack of redundancies in the FAA’s system could trigger catastrophic failures in other ways and touched off a blame game in Washington. "},{"_id":"YIN3O24JS5H75C6P7CV4OWUFYQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy seized on the chaos to hammer Congress, saying it had failed to pony up enough funding to pay for systemwide upgrades."},{"_id":"LW5P2ARVM5FO5KM3WKHWZOSHCE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he told reporters at the White House Friday night, asking that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project. Their lack of action, he said, had forced his department to pursue patchwork upgrades that were insufficient. It was a dramatic increase in his demand for additional money, which for the past several months has hovered at $30 billion."},{"_id":"JKJJSB67KRFI7FIFUG2HT4LALI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But lawmakers in both parties are raising questions about how efficiently Duffy and the FAA have been spending the money they have already been given."},{"_id":"XVI7SMPNFVBE5LUJWUREJWIXOM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said in a statement issued shortly after Duffy’s news conference, accusing the administration of failing to take responsibility for its failures in “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents.”"},{"_id":"M435G3S22ZHQLHO2IYAZFDQKU4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in t</i><a href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/ground-stop-air-traffic-faa.html\"><i>he New York Times</i></a><i>.</i>"}],"copyright":"Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. Post"}},{"content_elements":[{"_id":"7PJC3WMHWJBS7G4SPGXECKU4XM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Sterban, a backup vocalist for Elvis Presley who went on to international acclaim as the bass singer for the Oak Ridge Boys, the country vocal quartet for whom he sang the “oom-papa-mow-mow” refrain on the 1981 blockbuster hit “Elvira,” died on Saturday in Hendersonville, Tenn. He was 83."},{"_id":"NK55NA2QMJE2DFRZUX43CO4GYM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His death was confirmed by his family and the Oak Ridge Boys. They said that Mr. Sterban, who had cancer, had died of complications from bronchitis and pneumonia."},{"_id":"D3ZYKRM6MBECRNOSI5GIMVWJKE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A singer of extraordinary range and power, Mr. Sterban could hit notes so low they could only be felt, as opposed to heard. He also could hit notes higher than many tenors can reach. His basso profundo not only anchored the Oak Ridge Boys’ gospel-steeped sound; it carried the occasional melodic lead on recordings like the group’s 1979 remake of the Righteous Brothers’ Top 40 pop hit “Dream On.”"},{"_id":"2QVF3XBHKJBYBGLXZMBQINVXZ4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His reverberating vocals galvanized the Oaks’ version of “Elvira,” a song that had previously been recorded by artists including Rodney Crowell and Kenny Rogers and the First Edition."},{"_id":"OPNCSNW3V5C25MOB5UXXZI5SQE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"It was never more than a minor hit, though, until Sterban’s stentorian “oom-papa-mow-mow” (framed by shouts of “Giddy up!” and “Hi-ho Silver!”) transformed it into a Grammy Award-winning record, and one of the most inescapable earworms of the early 1980s."},{"_id":"HRNHVASFUVHYXAYNDSADAZM6PM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“It absolutely carried us to another stratosphere,” Mr. Sterban explained in his 2012 memoir, <i>From Elvis to Elvira: My Life on Stage</i>, written with Steven Robinson. “The song, especially the lines I sang, was seemingly on everyone’s lips. It was unbelievable.”"},{"_id":"4JPJDLARYJFHHIGKNWUFWGMGBY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With 2 million copies sold, “Elvira” topped the country chart, crossing over to the pop Top 10 and helping secure the Oaks’ reputation as one of the most popular vocal groups in the history of country music."},{"_id":"XK7FPDGUUJCD5KU4YUHGMM4SVI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Besides Mr. Sterban, the group’s classic lineup, formed in the early 1970s, included lead singer Duane Allen; tenor Joe Bonsall, who died in 2024; and baritone William Lee Golden."},{"_id":"UHKRRJKLRRGVHICURYJLNXLT2M","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The group was formed as a gospel quartet in Oak Ridge, Tenn., in the early 1940s, disbanding and reforming at least twice before Mr. Sterban and Bonsall teamed up with Allen and Golden, stabilizing what had long been a mercurial lineup. Over the next two decades, the four men modernized the group’s original gospel sound with pop-country elements, placing 17 singles at the top of the country chart and 17 others in the country Top 10."},{"_id":"B2Q6R5HFGRF5LNYYCLFWGVZWSI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With records like “Elvira” and “Bobbie Sue” (1982), Mr. Sterban and the Oaks infused traditional country harmony singing with techniques popularized by R&B vocal groups like the Coasters and the Dominoes. They also contributed vocals to the likes of Paul Simon’s 1977 Top 10 pop hit “Slip Slidin’ Away.”"},{"_id":"7KC4MP27MVF3ZAQVVHXPEUR6PE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This more far-reaching aesthetic was hardly second nature to the group, though — at least, not at first."},{"_id":"ERLXZSXC5BC57HQ6BRNC5IEREI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This was especially the case when, at a commercial low point in the mid-’70s before they found a larger country audience, they went into the studio to sing backup on Jimmy Buffett’s “My Head Hurts, My Feet Stink, and I Don’t Love Jesus.”"},{"_id":"CHIMK35RHRADFCVFWFOHHY75VM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"35UGSUHYGNDZFIVT2IGUP7VLKA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“What in the world had we gotten ourselves into?” Mr. Sterban wrote in his memoir, describing how the members of the group felt at the time. They had already been accused of being sellouts by their core gospel following for performing covers of hits by the Eagles and Olivia Newton-John in concert."},{"_id":"TUGCD3VDNBES3FLJHF3DKH3ZWI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“All we could imagine,” he added, “were headlines confirming what many of our detractors already seemed to believe: ‘Oak Ridge Boys don’t love Jesus!’”"},{"_id":"NBQIM2TYHJFKNOVWFN6FEEOABQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"J4YY5RJBDNDADIB7JJ7AYHU55Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Anthony Sterban was born on April 24, 1943, in Camden, N.J., one of three children of Edward and Victoria (Giordano) Sterban. The son of Polish immigrants, his father was an electrician. His mother, a native of Salandra, a township in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, worked various jobs, including at a chocolate factory."},{"_id":"LPA2NXMT7NCHTJTNI2LCHATV2A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The product of a strict religious upbringing, young Richard began singing at the local Assembly of God church at 6 and went on to play tuba, sousaphone, and an assortment of other brass instruments in high school. While attending Trenton State College (now the College of New Jersey), he majored in music before dropping out to form the Keystone Quartet, a gospel group, in the early 1960s."},{"_id":"ZUO6CJEHWNBVPKDGNRHWWFSPUI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Life on the road, though, didn’t agree with some of the quartet’s members, and the group split up in early 1965, at which time Mr. Sterban took a job selling menswear at the Gimbels department store in northeast Philadelphia."},{"_id":"UEXL5CY5BBC53LAD7ENK662LHY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Shortly before that, he married Sandra Wilson, with whom he had three sons, Rich, Chris, and Doug."},{"_id":"OZ2KOW47O5GXNB756FJ2YXKU54","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In 1970, Mr. Sterban was hired to sing bass in the touring edition of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet, one of the premier Southern Gospel groups of the day."},{"_id":"4E4VGKSSFRFORM7EWVS6WWQJIQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A year later, the Stamps were hired to be Presley’s background singers, appearing with him at his four shows at Madison Square Garden in June 1972, as well as during his five-week residency in Las Vegas later that summer."},{"_id":"R342YOK6FNGUNEQHHYDO53QFV4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Mr. Sterban also sang on major recordings by Presley including “Burning Love,” a No. 2 pop hit in 1972, and “Always on My Mind.”"},{"_id":"5VCPEDP6DRAZRE4AGJHM7YFGBQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In October 1972, seizing the chance to be part of a headlining act of his own, Mr. Sterban accepted an invitation to join the Oak Ridge Boys, replacing bass singer Noel Fox."},{"_id":"HIAJ2BYFEZHRJEFNENKJAAFXPE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The newly reconstituted quartet initially struggled to make it in the country market. Buoyed, though, by a stint as regulars in Johnny Cash’s touring revue, they finally broke through to a wider audience with “Y’all Come Back Saloon.” A Top 10 country single in 1977, the record inaugurated a decade-plus string of hits that paved the way for sold-out concert tours, regular appearances on late-night television shows, and five Grammy Awards."},{"_id":"RXORM4FKIBEBJACWZ4L5CFH5HM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Oak Ridge Boys were inducted into the Gospel Hall of Fame in 2000 and into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015."},{"_id":"LI3YAWLWRVFB3DIJJAY57GSGZM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"An avid sports fan, Mr. Sterban was for years a part owner of — and occasional color commentator for — the Nashville Sounds baseball team, the Triple-A minor league affiliate of the Milwaukee Brewers. He also did color commentary for Vanderbilt University’s men’s baseball team."},{"_id":"KO7DW2YO2RCBHOZ66NNPOKUBNQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In addition to his sons from his first marriage, which ended in divorce, Mr. Sterban is survived by his second wife, Donna (Summers) Sterban; their daughters, Tori and Lauren; and several grandchildren."},{"_id":"RYQX5HPVEZHSHPN247LHATDMLE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"FYXJS5SOUFAPHDJHDO7JFO5DW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Their early struggles to find their stylistic equilibrium notwithstanding, the Oak Ridge Boys nevertheless continued to push the boundaries of country music decades after they found success with a more wide-ranging approach."},{"_id":"HLQ4WV4ILNDJHE4E3CUTRUSVEE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Maybe nowhere was this more evident than in their haunting 2009 rendition of the White Stripes’ 2003 single “Seven Nation Army.” Recorded with producer Dave Cobb, whose clients include Jason Isbell and Lady Gaga, the collaboration has been likened to Cash’s partnership with iconoclastic producer Rick Rubin."},{"_id":"IAI4HW7Q5RB5LES6KHYRB52JPY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“I think Dave took us down some roads we might not have traveled on our own,” Mr. Sterban was quoted as saying about the experience on the group’s website. “The music may be different, but he did not try to change us; he challenged us.”"},{"_id":"YB6JGHDCKFFPLCDB25PPHTEIKU","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in </i><a — The nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening has highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure that has had several disruptive failures in recent months."},{"_id":"TKCGDRBHAFF3VL6UHVDK7AYQKY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Officials called the rare ground stop after outdated communications lines became overloaded and began to fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin."},{"_id":"FZOF62F64NGKLEH4ZJA2WSEY5Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The breakdown occurred less than two months after a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush International Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line."},{"_id":"KHKDJEBNPBEXRJ2IHKVQV2HNFY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the FAA has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. The FAA has yet to identify precisely what caused communication lines to falter."},{"_id":"JIGMDC7ICJEYBKHOIXOMNM5XIA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Associated Press reported that Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said Saturday that the U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of today. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”"},{"_id":"YNB7FWHTTNH4HCZI6C7VXIL2XQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said."},{"_id":"DFIKVJG35JEFJGLK45KPK2R74A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause."},{"_id":"QPKYH6LC3FG6NM6YFT3OFZA2PI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment,” Duffy said."},{"_id":"5NEDTLYXOZBLLNUDK2NKRHVJ7E","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the successive episodes of such problems have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that continue to hamper air traffic controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after concerted efforts to make improvements. And they raised questions about whether the federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems and redundancies to prevent disruptive or even catastrophic failures."},{"_id":"BNMOUXOZTJD3RP2MRJYRKHKNXM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"For decades, air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks, and alphabetical keyboards so old that the FAA has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to help pay for upgrades, after a series of outages in air traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, caused alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities."},{"_id":"LSZ4PGSALZDSBO7T45UN6CBGQY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecoms contractor tasked to manage the system upgrades, boasted on its website that it had converted about 70% of the copper line to fiber optic cable; last week, the FAA announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks."},{"_id":"Q6KS2XJEOFGV7FBDZETY33EUCI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the disruptions in recent weeks showed that those upgrades had serious vulnerabilities themselves."},{"_id":"E6BY4EP4HZBC5BTBVRQ2HDUTHQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered — to their surprise — had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later."},{"_id":"LSIQDWL3BZGHNFAPIYBN65E7AY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A similar incident occurred in October at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina, when a contractor working on plumbing accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. Just one day after that, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush International Airport, when yet another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line."},{"_id":"4Y5DCM5WBBFX7KO6TLENUQAHW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The fiber line upgrades themselves, Bedford, the FAA administrator, told reporters at the time, were not enough to save the system from failure."},{"_id":"ZQ54KCD6YZE4JPTQDGUFG2HSY4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Ideally, the FAA wanted to put data into cloud services, he told reporters then, so that “when you have a fiber cut, you have multiple pathways of backup.”"},{"_id":"FNIXXMAUH5A7BIE6SLYLM4ILQQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today we have physical fiber and when it’s cut, there’s one redundancy, and when we lose that, there’s no more redundancy,” he added."},{"_id":"LKQ6CSVCTZDJZL6OIZMOBBATOQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Friday’s national ground stop revealed that the lack of redundancies in the FAA’s system could trigger catastrophic failures in other ways and touched off a blame game in Washington. "},{"_id":"YIN3O24JS5H75C6P7CV4OWUFYQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy seized on the chaos to hammer Congress, saying it had failed to pony up enough funding to pay for systemwide upgrades."},{"_id":"LW5P2ARVM5FO5KM3WKHWZOSHCE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he told reporters at the White House Friday night, asking that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project. Their lack of action, he said, had forced his department to pursue patchwork upgrades that were insufficient. It was a dramatic increase in his demand for additional money, which for the past several months has hovered at $30 billion."},{"_id":"JKJJSB67KRFI7FIFUG2HT4LALI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But lawmakers in both parties are raising questions about how efficiently Duffy and the FAA have been spending the money they have already been given."},{"_id":"XVI7SMPNFVBE5LUJWUREJWIXOM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said in a statement issued shortly after Duffy’s news conference, accusing the administration of failing to take responsibility for its failures in “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents.”"},{"_id":"M435G3S22ZHQLHO2IYAZFDQKU4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in t</i><a href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/ground-stop-air-traffic-faa.html\"><i>he New York Times</i></a><i>.</i>"}],"copyright":"Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. Post"}},{"content_elements":[{"_id":"7PJC3WMHWJBS7G4SPGXECKU4XM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Sterban, a backup vocalist for Elvis Presley who went on to international acclaim as the bass singer for the Oak Ridge Boys, the country vocal quartet for whom he sang the “oom-papa-mow-mow” refrain on the 1981 blockbuster hit “Elvira,” died on Saturday in Hendersonville, Tenn. He was 83."},{"_id":"NK55NA2QMJE2DFRZUX43CO4GYM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His death was confirmed by his family and the Oak Ridge Boys. They said that Mr. Sterban, who had cancer, had died of complications from bronchitis and pneumonia."},{"_id":"D3ZYKRM6MBECRNOSI5GIMVWJKE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A singer of extraordinary range and power, Mr. Sterban could hit notes so low they could only be felt, as opposed to heard. He also could hit notes higher than many tenors can reach. His basso profundo not only anchored the Oak Ridge Boys’ gospel-steeped sound; it carried the occasional melodic lead on recordings like the group’s 1979 remake of the Righteous Brothers’ Top 40 pop hit “Dream On.”"},{"_id":"2QVF3XBHKJBYBGLXZMBQINVXZ4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His reverberating vocals galvanized the Oaks’ version of “Elvira,” a song that had previously been recorded by artists including Rodney Crowell and Kenny Rogers and the First Edition."},{"_id":"OPNCSNW3V5C25MOB5UXXZI5SQE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"It was never more than a minor hit, though, until Sterban’s stentorian “oom-papa-mow-mow” (framed by shouts of “Giddy up!” and “Hi-ho Silver!”) transformed it into a Grammy Award-winning record, and one of the most inescapable earworms of the early 1980s."},{"_id":"HRNHVASFUVHYXAYNDSADAZM6PM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“It absolutely carried us to another stratosphere,” Mr. Sterban explained in his 2012 memoir, <i>From Elvis to Elvira: My Life on Stage</i>, written with Steven Robinson. “The song, especially the lines I sang, was seemingly on everyone’s lips. It was unbelievable.”"},{"_id":"4JPJDLARYJFHHIGKNWUFWGMGBY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With 2 million copies sold, “Elvira” topped the country chart, crossing over to the pop Top 10 and helping secure the Oaks’ reputation as one of the most popular vocal groups in the history of country music."},{"_id":"XK7FPDGUUJCD5KU4YUHGMM4SVI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Besides Mr. Sterban, the group’s classic lineup, formed in the early 1970s, included lead singer Duane Allen; tenor Joe Bonsall, who died in 2024; and baritone William Lee Golden."},{"_id":"UHKRRJKLRRGVHICURYJLNXLT2M","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The group was formed as a gospel quartet in Oak Ridge, Tenn., in the early 1940s, disbanding and reforming at least twice before Mr. Sterban and Bonsall teamed up with Allen and Golden, stabilizing what had long been a mercurial lineup. Over the next two decades, the four men modernized the group’s original gospel sound with pop-country elements, placing 17 singles at the top of the country chart and 17 others in the country Top 10."},{"_id":"B2Q6R5HFGRF5LNYYCLFWGVZWSI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With records like “Elvira” and “Bobbie Sue” (1982), Mr. Sterban and the Oaks infused traditional country harmony singing with techniques popularized by R&B vocal groups like the Coasters and the Dominoes. They also contributed vocals to the likes of Paul Simon’s 1977 Top 10 pop hit “Slip Slidin’ Away.”"},{"_id":"7KC4MP27MVF3ZAQVVHXPEUR6PE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This more far-reaching aesthetic was hardly second nature to the group, though — at least, not at first."},{"_id":"ERLXZSXC5BC57HQ6BRNC5IEREI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This was especially the case when, at a commercial low point in the mid-’70s before they found a larger country audience, they went into the studio to sing backup on Jimmy Buffett’s “My Head Hurts, My Feet Stink, and I Don’t Love Jesus.”"},{"_id":"CHIMK35RHRADFCVFWFOHHY75VM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"35UGSUHYGNDZFIVT2IGUP7VLKA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“What in the world had we gotten ourselves into?” Mr. Sterban wrote in his memoir, describing how the members of the group felt at the time. They had already been accused of being sellouts by their core gospel following for performing covers of hits by the Eagles and Olivia Newton-John in concert."},{"_id":"TUGCD3VDNBES3FLJHF3DKH3ZWI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“All we could imagine,” he added, “were headlines confirming what many of our detractors already seemed to believe: ‘Oak Ridge Boys don’t love Jesus!’”"},{"_id":"NBQIM2TYHJFKNOVWFN6FEEOABQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"J4YY5RJBDNDADIB7JJ7AYHU55Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Anthony Sterban was born on April 24, 1943, in Camden, N.J., one of three children of Edward and Victoria (Giordano) Sterban. The son of Polish immigrants, his father was an electrician. His mother, a native of Salandra, a township in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, worked various jobs, including at a chocolate factory."},{"_id":"LPA2NXMT7NCHTJTNI2LCHATV2A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The product of a strict religious upbringing, young Richard began singing at the local Assembly of God church at 6 and went on to play tuba, sousaphone, and an assortment of other brass instruments in high school. While attending Trenton State College (now the College of New Jersey), he majored in music before dropping out to form the Keystone Quartet, a gospel group, in the early 1960s."},{"_id":"ZUO6CJEHWNBVPKDGNRHWWFSPUI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Life on the road, though, didn’t agree with some of the quartet’s members, and the group split up in early 1965, at which time Mr. Sterban took a job selling menswear at the Gimbels department store in northeast Philadelphia."},{"_id":"UEXL5CY5BBC53LAD7ENK662LHY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Shortly before that, he married Sandra Wilson, with whom he had three sons, Rich, Chris, and Doug."},{"_id":"OZ2KOW47O5GXNB756FJ2YXKU54","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In 1970, Mr. Sterban was hired to sing bass in the touring edition of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet, one of the premier Southern Gospel groups of the day."},{"_id":"4E4VGKSSFRFORM7EWVS6WWQJIQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A year later, the Stamps were hired to be Presley’s background singers, appearing with him at his four shows at Madison Square Garden in June 1972, as well as during his five-week residency in Las Vegas later that summer."},{"_id":"R342YOK6FNGUNEQHHYDO53QFV4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Mr. Sterban also sang on major recordings by Presley including “Burning Love,” a No. 2 pop hit in 1972, and “Always on My Mind.”"},{"_id":"5VCPEDP6DRAZRE4AGJHM7YFGBQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In October 1972, seizing the chance to be part of a headlining act of his own, Mr. Sterban accepted an invitation to join the Oak Ridge Boys, replacing bass singer Noel Fox."},{"_id":"HIAJ2BYFEZHRJEFNENKJAAFXPE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The newly reconstituted quartet initially struggled to make it in the country market. Buoyed, though, by a stint as regulars in Johnny Cash’s touring revue, they finally broke through to a wider audience with “Y’all Come Back Saloon.” A Top 10 country single in 1977, the record inaugurated a decade-plus string of hits that paved the way for sold-out concert tours, regular appearances on late-night television shows, and five Grammy Awards."},{"_id":"RXORM4FKIBEBJACWZ4L5CFH5HM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Oak Ridge Boys were inducted into the Gospel Hall of Fame in 2000 and into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015."},{"_id":"LI3YAWLWRVFB3DIJJAY57GSGZM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"An avid sports fan, Mr. Sterban was for years a part owner of — and occasional color commentator for — the Nashville Sounds baseball team, the Triple-A minor league affiliate of the Milwaukee Brewers. He also did color commentary for Vanderbilt University’s men’s baseball team."},{"_id":"KO7DW2YO2RCBHOZ66NNPOKUBNQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In addition to his sons from his first marriage, which ended in divorce, Mr. Sterban is survived by his second wife, Donna (Summers) Sterban; their daughters, Tori and Lauren; and several grandchildren."},{"_id":"RYQX5HPVEZHSHPN247LHATDMLE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"FYXJS5SOUFAPHDJHDO7JFO5DW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Their early struggles to find their stylistic equilibrium notwithstanding, the Oak Ridge Boys nevertheless continued to push the boundaries of country music decades after they found success with a more wide-ranging approach."},{"_id":"HLQ4WV4ILNDJHE4E3CUTRUSVEE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Maybe nowhere was this more evident than in their haunting 2009 rendition of the White Stripes’ 2003 single “Seven Nation Army.” Recorded with producer Dave Cobb, whose clients include Jason Isbell and Lady Gaga, the collaboration has been likened to Cash’s partnership with iconoclastic producer Rick Rubin."},{"_id":"IAI4HW7Q5RB5LES6KHYRB52JPY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“I think Dave took us down some roads we might not have traveled on our own,” Mr. Sterban was quoted as saying about the experience on the group’s website. “The music may be different, but he did not try to change us; he challenged us.”"},{"_id":"YB6JGHDCKFFPLCDB25PPHTEIKU","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in </i><a ","type":"text"},{"content":"Malayshia Allford’s parents were arguing in the parking lot of a Springfield Township strip mall when someone called police. Her mother tried to board a SEPTA bus with the girl — but her<b> </b>father pulled them back to the sidewalk. Then, he struck the mother in the head, police said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"That 2020 incident, and the investigations that followed, prompted a caseworker to remove Malayshia, then just 4 years old, from her mother’s home in Philadelphia. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Over the next six years of her short and tumultuous life, she would be shuffled through at least three homes by Philadelphia’s child-welfare system. On Nov. 5, one of those foster parents, <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-alford-body-found-new-jersey-20261105.html?_gl=1*v292av*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTEzOTk3MDExOC4xNzk0NTc3NzQ0*_ga_8ER3Q26BL0*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgxODkxMTIyMjU5*_ga_9HHXKD70G8*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgyMDg3OTY0ODk0\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-alford-body-found-new-jersey-20261105.html?_gl=1*v292av*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTEzOTk3MDExOC4xNzk0NTc3NzQ0*_ga_8ER3Q26BL0*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgxODkxMTIyMjU5*_ga_9HHXKD70G8*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgyMDg3OTY0ODk0\">Carprice Williams, was charged</a> with killing the 10-year-old girl and leaving her body in the trunk of a car. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Williams was a Philadelphia fifth-grade teacher whose disciplinary style, including withholding lunch from students, worried colleagues and drew complaints from some children and parents. She had been a foster mother to at least four children dating back to 2019 or earlier. In 2021, another child who was placed in her care was hospitalized with what a doctor <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-alford-carprice-williams-history-of-abuse-20261106.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-alford-carprice-williams-history-of-abuse-20261106.html\">deemed near-fatal injuries</a>. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The story of how their paths collided raises serious questions about the systems the city and state have in place to keep children safe, and to vet those who care for them. ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Years in the system","type":"header"},{"content":"Some of Malayshia’s relatives had not seen the child since she was a 4-year-old with a heart-melting smile and an affinity for Minnie Mouse. That’s how long she had been in the child-welfare system. ","type":"text"},{"content":"A caseworker had temporarily removed Malayshia from her mother’s home after the domestic incident. In April 2021, a Philadelphia Family Court judge found the home unsafe, noting that drugs had been found in the child’s bedroom and that the mother failed to seek care after she suspected her daughter had been sexually abused. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Malayshia was placed with a relative, and allowed weekly supervised visits with her parents. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The court noted that Malayshia’s parents, Everine Brown-Ward and Nazir Allford, had not cooperated with the child-welfare agency, and had sent threatening messages, including a shooting threat, to the relative who was caring for the child. The father also assaulted a child-welfare caseworker, according to court records. Allford’s brother, Nafis Horne, said the parents were grieving and not ready to comment.","type":"text"},{"content":"A lawyer, Michael Graves Jr., was appointed to represent Malayshia’s interests, according to court records dating to 2021. Graves did not respond to messages.","type":"text"},{"content":"Frank Cervone, who for years led the Support Center for Child Advocates, said his office and the city’s public defender both require lawyers to conduct twice-a-year in-home visits. But there are no such standards for private, court-appointed lawyers such as Graves. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“Most of them simply don’t do that,” Cervone said. “They don’t see it as part of their practice.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"In 2022, both parents were arrested after taking Malayshia from a supervised visit at Catholic Community Services in Northeast Philadelphia. Both pleaded guilty to interfering with custody. After that, they no longer were allowed visits, relatives said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Still, multiple family members said, there were other options for the girl, who had three siblings — two in foster homes, and one living with a maternal aunt, Yolanda Brown. ","type":"text"},{"content":"By last year, Malayshia was in a different foster home. But caseworkers found that she was physically and sexually abused there, according to Nadeem Bezar, a lawyer representing Malayshia’s estate. ","type":"text"},{"content":"That’s why she was removed from that home and placed with Williams, he said.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"‘The care just wasn’t there’","type":"header"},{"content":"A fifth-grade teacher at Lewis C. Cassidy Academics Plus in Overbrook, Williams, 36, was known as a disciplinarian with what some coworkers described as an imperious attitude. ","type":"text"},{"content":"She demanded to be called Dr. Williams, according to two coworkers and a parent, and touted a doctoral degree from Drexel University on her LinkedIn page. Asked to confirm that, a Drexel spokesperson said only that Williams had earned a master’s degree from the university in 2015.","type":"text"},{"content":"A parent and a school staffer both said they had complained to the principal about what they viewed as harassment by Williams, and believed others had as well. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Cassidy parent Justin Forte said Williams seemed frazzled by her large class and ill-equipped to manage behavioral issues.","type":"text"},{"content":"“She wasn’t handling things right,” said Forte, who said Williams had singled his 11-year-old son out for reprimands and repeatedly prevented him from eating lunch, in violation of district policy.","type":"text"},{"content":"“The first thing a teacher’s supposed to do is care for children,” he said, “and it seems like the care just wasn’t there.”","type":"text"},{"content":"Stephen Ford, who taught fifth grade alongside Williams, said she was an effective teacher, but stern. While some other teachers try to infuse teaching with humor, he said, “I didn’t hear a lot of laughing in her room.”","type":"text"},{"content":"A Cassidy gym teacher, Corey Blakey, who also runs after-school and summer programs, said Williams repeatedly punished students in her class by forcing them to spend their lunch period in her classroom. He said the principal ended up warning her against such discipline. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Cassidy principal Herman Douglas did not respond to a request for comment.","type":"text"},{"content":"“She’s really possessive,” Blakey said, adding that she urged students not to join an enrichment program and told him to remove certain students from after-school programs. ","type":"text"},{"content":"After observing a tense altercation between Williams and another staffer, Blakey urged the other staffer to file a complaint, he said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Williams attended Lower Merion High School and Rosemont College, and was first licensed as a teacher in Pennsylvania in 2013.","type":"text"},{"content":"She was hired by the Philadelphia School District as a substitute in 2015, taught at Young Scholars Charter School for the 2015-16 school year, and was a district teacher from 2017 through 2023, including at Thomas Mifflin School in East Falls. Philadelphia School District officials declined to provide further details about her postings or to comment.","type":"text"},{"content":"A former friend of Williams’, whose daughter was in the teacher’s fifth-grade class at Mifflin, said troubling patterns were apparent back then: Williams was harsh with some children, but overly involved with others, ordering them UberEats to her classroom and hosting them in her home.","type":"text"},{"content":"The friend, who asked not to be identified because she did not want to be associated with Williams’ alleged criminal conduct, said her daughter and some peers were enthralled with the teacher because she was “was more on their level. If they talked to each other crazy, she did it, too.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"Then, while visiting her home, the woman said, Williams punched her daughter with a closed fist. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“I put Carprice out of my house when she punched her,” the friend said.","type":"text"},{"content":"In 2019, Williams took in a 14-year-old foster daughter, Maria Campbell, who said Williams punished her for taking snacks — locking her in her room during the pandemic for what seemed like months and forcing her to write out an apology over and over. When she got the chance, Campbell, now 21, said, she ran away and never saw Williams again. ","type":"text"},{"content":"On June 27, 2020, Williams took in two foster children in her rented rowhouse on Simpson Street in West Philadelphia. Six months later, records show, they were removed after one was hospitalized with severe brain bleeds, malnutrition, and vitamin deficiencies that a doctor said indicated that food had been withheld. Because of the apparent abuse and neglect, a state “near fatality” review team recommended that Williams “never be permitted to care for other foster children.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"Police investigated, according to the state review, but made no arrests because the child did not disclose what caused the hemorrhaging. In October, according to a lawsuit that did not name Williams and was later settled out of court, a child protective services report laid out detailed allegations of abuse by Williams — grabbing a child by the braids and slamming her head to the floor, smacking her in the face, forcing her to squat for long stretches. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Yet, the state review team report, finalized more than a year later in November 2022, makes no mention of that information. A state spokesperson said Williams had successfully appealed the finding of child abuse and had her record expunged.","type":"text"},{"content":"Though the state maintains a <a href=\"https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/dhs/documents/adoptpakids/documents/Act%20160%20Bulletin.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">registry of foster care providers</a>, it is not clear if the information about that incident made it into the registry. Nor is it clear whether the Family Court judge, the Philadelphia Department of Human Services (DHS), or the foster care agency that certified Williams consulted that database. The agency, Pennsylvania Mentor, did not respond to requests for comment. Philadelphia DHS Commissioner Kimberly Ali said Saturday that she could not comment on any individual case, but that under state law it is the foster agency that is in charge of approving caregivers.","type":"text"},{"content":"By early 2025, Williams had a young son of her own and was hired at Cassidy. And that summer, she took in another foster child, Malayshia.","type":"text"},{"content":"She called the little girl May May. And, according to her friend, Williams said she had plans to adopt the child.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"‘A really good kid’","type":"header"},{"content":"This spring, according to Blakey, Williams asked to enroll Malayshia in summer programs he runs at the school and with the Tiger Woods Foundation. That is when he got a chance to meet the girl.","type":"text"},{"content":"Blakey was impressed by the 10-year-old’s enthusiasm and curiosity. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“She was not a perfect student, but near to that. She was happy-go-lucky. She wanted to be in the program. She wanted to do all the activities. She wanted to do everything,” he said. “She was a really good kid.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"But Malayshia did not show up at Robert E. Lamberton School on Friday, Oct. 23.","type":"text"},{"content":"Over that weekend, two witnesses who visited the home saw the child in bed, not moving, according to a police report. Williams did not report the girl missing until Monday afternoon. And when she did, she told Malayshia’s aunt that the girl’s parents had taken her. ","type":"text"},{"content":"As police, FBI, relatives, and neighbors began a frantic search, according to the report, Williams <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/carprice-williams-cassidy-teacher-fake-texts-20261109.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/carprice-williams-cassidy-teacher-fake-texts-20261109.html\">faked affectionate texts to cover her tracks</a>. One phony text from Malayshia read, “Mommy I know you are waiting for me to come home but my family they don’t want me to be adopted. … I love you.” ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Days later, investigators identified a man caught on video leaving Williams’ home dragging a cumbersome, oddly shaped bag with a long strand of braided hair trailing from it. The man, a relative of Williams’, eventually led them to a car parked in Lindenwold, South Jersey. Malayshia’s body — bruised and battered, with a fractured rib and whiplike marks on her legs — was in the trunk.","type":"text"},{"content":"Witnesses later told police that Williams had thrown Malayshia down stairs, beaten her with a phone cord, deprived her of food, and forced her to wear a heavy vest and walk up and down the stairs. Williams denied that, telling police that the vest was only calming, and that Malayshia might have fallen but was not pushed. ","type":"text"},{"content":"In the days since, <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-allford-philadelphia-foster-care-mayor-cherelle-parker-20261111.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-allford-philadelphia-foster-care-mayor-cherelle-parker-20261111.html\">City Council members have called for hearings</a>, Mayor Cherelle L. Parker has announced a systemwide review, and the district attorney’s office has <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-alford-body-found-new-jersey-20261105.html?_gl=1*v292av*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTEzOTk3MDExOC4xNzk0NTc3NzQ0*_ga_8ER3Q26BL0*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgxODkxMTIyMjU5*_ga_9HHXKD70G8*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgyMDg3OTY0ODk0\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/crime/malayshia-alford-body-found-new-jersey-20261105.html?_gl=1*v292av*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTEzOTk3MDExOC4xNzk0NTc3NzQ0*_ga_8ER3Q26BL0*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgxODkxMTIyMjU5*_ga_9HHXKD70G8*czE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ1Nzc3NDQkajYwJGwwJGgyMDg3OTY0ODk0\">charged Williams with murder</a>.","type":"text"},{"content":"But Malayshia’s relatives said they are still trying to understand how a failure this profound was possible. ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Last weekend, more than 200 people gathered in Morris Park in Overbrook to release balloons in Malayshia’s memory. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Nafis Horne, her paternal uncle, said he would have gladly taken in his niece. But no officials ever reached out, he said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"He said his sister, Nyfisha Allford, had sought custody of the little girl but got nowhere, despite <a href=\"https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dhs/resources/keep-kids-safe/family-first#accordion-b4b45c758b-item-9fb855fa02\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">city and state policies</a> prioritizing placements with relatives over foster care. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“My sister tried to get her,” Horne said, “but that fell through the cracks.”","type":"text"},{"content":"<i>Staff writers Ellie Rushing, Jillian Kramer, and Jesse Bunch contributed to this article.</i>","type":"text"}],"credits":{"by":[{"_id":"melamed_samantha","description":"I'm a reporter on the Investigations Team, digging into stories about how injustice, corruption, and government dysfunction impact Philadelphians — and exploring what we can do about it. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Kane, Philly’s answer to Walter Cronkite during the golden age of local news, retired from broadcasting today at 84.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Kane, who worked at all three major networks in the city and transformed nightly news with his catchphrase — “The big story on Action News” — was king of the airwaves when anchormen were civic institutions and celebrities. When local news was appointment viewing and ratings and rivalries roared.","type":"text"},{"content":"At 27, he became the youngest major-market television news anchor in America, and eventually the only Philly anchor to helm all three major networks. Proudly Jewish, <a href=\"https://www.phillymag.com/news/2005/06/01/my-philadelphia-story-larry-kane/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">he said in 2005</a> that he once battled doubts he could succeed in a town that was “really run by the white Protestant establishment.”","type":"text"},{"content":"He rode shotgun with the Beatles during <a href=\"http://google.com/search?q=larry+kane+and+the+beatle+sinquirer&rlz=1C1GCEA_enUS1222US1222&oq=larry+kane+and+the+beatle+sinquirer&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIJCAEQIRgKGKABMgkIAhAhGAoYoAEyCQgDECEYChigATIJCAQQIRgKGKABMgcIBRAhGI8C0gEINzcxMGowajeoAgCwAgA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">the fever pitch of Beatlemania</a>. Covered presidents and popes and world leaders. And endless Philadelphia triumph and tragedy. He witnessed Philadelphia bomb itself.","type":"text"},{"content":"For nearly 60 years, Larry Kane told Philadelphians the news — and why it mattered. And <a href=\"https://www.larrykane.com/home/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Philadelphians believed him</a>.","type":"text"},{"content":"Before his farewell broadcast Sunday on KYW Newsradio, where he has offered commentary for over two decades, the iconic newsman issued a warning about attacks on the media and <a href=\"https://www.audacy.com/kywnewsradio/news/local/philadelphia-broadcaster-larry-kane-retires\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">the slow erosion of local journalism</a>.","type":"text"},{"content":"“It’s all about local news,” Kane told me. “If people don’t have local news, they can’t understand what’s going on around them.","type":"text"},{"content":"I’ll be reporting more on Kane’s singular career in the coming weeks — and would love to include some of your favorite Larry stories. Share them with me at mnewall@inquirer.com.","type":"text"},{"content":"For now, let’s hear from Larry.","type":"text"},{"content":"<b>Mike: </b>You were the only broadcast journalist to travel to every stop on <a href=\"https://www.larrykane.com/ticket-to-ride/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.larrykane.com/ticket-to-ride/\">the Beatles 1964 and 1965 North American tours</a>. It was an assignment you famously almost turned down. ","type":"text"},{"content":"<b>Larry: </b>The first time I met them, I went down there to their room. I was wearing a suit and a skinny tie. Very conservative. Cohen, the former Comcast executive and U.S. ambassador to Canada who has been attempting to broker an agreement.","type":"text"},{"content":"For the first time in weeks, pulling back the curtain on what have been confidential talks, Cohen and leaders of both Drexel and the Academy shared details of the negotiations and their perceptions of the sticking points.","type":"text"},{"content":"Cohen said in an interview last week that talks broke off after the Academy said it wanted to pursue disaffiliation from Drexel but the two sides disagreed on terms. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The stalemate continues even as the university and the Academy announced Friday that they would accept a <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-natural-sciences-drexel-museum-funding-william-penn-foundations-20261113.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-natural-sciences-drexel-museum-funding-william-penn-foundations-20261113.html\">review funded by the William Penn Foundation</a> and other foundations for wide-ranging feasibility studies on the physical and fiscal conditions of the Academy and a sustainable model for its future. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The negotiations on the governance and fiscal structure of the Academy, however, are separate from the review, Drexel president Antonio Merlo said in a Friday interview. ","type":"text"},{"content":"On Monday, City Council will begin the second part of a <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/education/academy-natural-sciences-closure-philadelphia-city-council-20261026.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/education/academy-natural-sciences-closure-philadelphia-city-council-20261026.html\">hearing</a> investigating the shutdown of the Academy’s museum, with Merlo and Deputy Mayor Patricia Wellenbach — <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/city-council-subpoena-academy-natural-sciences-drexel-wellenbach-merlo-20261030.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/city-council-subpoena-academy-natural-sciences-drexel-wellenbach-merlo-20261030.html\">who were subpoenaed</a> by Council — scheduled to testify. The <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/education/academy-of-natural-sciences-closing-museum-philadelphia-20260901.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/education/academy-of-natural-sciences-closing-museum-philadelphia-20260901.html\">museum closed</a> to the public on Sept. 27, drawing <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-natural-sciences-museum-protest-philadelphia-20260908.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-natural-sciences-museum-protest-philadelphia-20260908.html\">outrage and protest</a> by community activists and Academy proponents. ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Cohen said Council’s steps have “interfered with” the negotiations between Drexel and the Academy. “The public vilification and witch hunt that we’re engaged in now is not constructive to coming up with a solution,” he said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Councilmember Isaiah Thomas, who leads the committee running the hearing, declined to address Cohen’s comments. But he said he has been involved in a lot of positive conversations with people who want to step up and save the Academy. There are multiple donors willing to put up “tens of millions of dollars” once the Academy’s path is clear, he said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“The biggest holdup now is Drexel and the Academy defining their relationship,” he said.","type":"text"},{"content":"<a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-natural-sciences-museum-drexel-university-20261007.html?_gl=1*etfmg7*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTc1MTI2NjkxLjE3OTQ2MzYwNDE.*_ga_8ER3Q26BL0*czE3OTQ2MzYwNDAkbzEkZzEkdDE3OTQ2MzYwODMkajE3JGwwJGgxNjgyNDQwNTA0*_ga_9HHXKD70G8*czE3OTQ2MzYwNDEkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ2MzYwODMkajE4JGwwJGgxMzgyMTg3OTA1\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noreferrer\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-natural-sciences-museum-drexel-university-20261007.html?_gl=1*etfmg7*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTc1MTI2NjkxLjE3OTQ2MzYwNDE.*_ga_8ER3Q26BL0*czE3OTQ2MzYwNDAkbzEkZzEkdDE3OTQ2MzYwODMkajE3JGwwJGgxNjgyNDQwNTA0*_ga_9HHXKD70G8*czE3OTQ2MzYwNDEkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTQ2MzYwODMkajE4JGwwJGgxMzgyMTg3OTA1\">Donors</a>, he said, do not want to commit until they know the status of the Academy and Drexel. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“If I’m a philanthropist and there’s not clarity on what you’re doing moving forward, why would I donate now? Am I donating to the Academy or am I donating to Drexel University? I’ll donate when I get clarity …” ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"A disputed ‘term sheet’","type":"header"},{"content":"Less than a year ago, Gov. Josh Shapiro and Mayor Cherelle L. Parker asked Cohen to help with the negotiations between Drexel and the Academy. Drexel had wanted the Academy, which it felt had become a financial drain, to <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/drexel-university-academy-of-natural-sciences-affiliation-20260410.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/drexel-university-academy-of-natural-sciences-affiliation-20260410.html\">fully merge into the university or disaffiliate</a>. ","type":"text"},{"content":"When talks lagged in July, Drexel threatened to cut off funding to the Academy, which would have “summarily put the Academy out of business,” according to Academy board chairperson Suzanne Biemiller.","type":"text"},{"content":"Cohen said he had brokered a “term sheet” that both sides had signed off on in September. It would have allowed for the “survival and healthy existence” of the Academy, he said. When it came time to negotiate “definitive documentation to implement the terms,” the two sides traded “competing proposals,” which Cohen said he did not think were that much at odds. ","type":"text"},{"content":"But after he called a meeting in early October to discuss the proposals, the Academy had changed its position and said it no longer wanted to implement the terms but instead pursue disaffiliation from Drexel, Cohen said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“They essentially reneged on the agreement that was reached in good faith,” Merlo said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Biemiller disagreed with that characterization. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“We said that the term sheet did not work economically and that the trustees of the Academy would therefore not approve it,” she said. She added that Drexel’s initial rejection of an offer by the William Penn Foundation to fund operating expenses of the Academy to keep the museum open “signaled to the Academy trustees that Drexel wasn’t working in the best interest of the Academy.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"The Academy, Cohen said, believed it could generate enough support through philanthropy, “new partners,” and government funding to stand on its own.","type":"text"},{"content":"He, the mayor, and the governor were all “skeptical” of that position. Biemiller countered that trustees have heard from a number of individuals and civic leaders who want to help the Academy. ","type":"text"},{"content":"(Shapiro’s spokesperson did not provide comment; neither did Parker’s.) ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Disaffiliate or fully merge?","type":"header"},{"content":"Cohen said he had been advising the parties against <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-of-natural-sciences-drexel-philadelphia-museum-closed-20261002.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/arts/academy-of-natural-sciences-drexel-philadelphia-museum-closed-20261002.html\">disaffiliation</a> and toward a full merger. But Merlo, he said, agreed to honor the Academy’s request for disaffiliation. The university offered to provide in-kind services for three months after the date of disaffiliation, Merlo said.<b> </b>","type":"text"},{"content":"The Academy, Cohen said, rejected that proposal and offered its own, which he characterized as “a bit … inflammatory.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"“It was not really a disaffiliation proposal because it did provide for significant additional financial support and in-kind support and continuation of educational and research support” from Drexel, Cohen said.","type":"text"},{"content":"The Academy, Merlo said, wanted Drexel’s continued financial support for five years. Neither Cohen nor Merlo would say how much the Academy requested, though Cohen said it was “a lot.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"The financial support from Drexel eventually would have ceased, Cohen said, but some of the in-kind support would have continued in perpetuity.","type":"text"},{"content":"The Academy’s proposal, he said, also called for the “immediate termination of all of the governance rights and financial controls and budgetary controls that Drexel has under the terms of the 2011 affiliation agreement.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"Cohen said he advised the Academy to modify its proposal and it declined. Drexel, Merlo said, rejected the Academy’s proposal and made a counteroffer.","type":"text"},{"content":"“We haven’t heard back ever since,” Merlo said.","type":"text"},{"content":"For him, disaffiliation meant that the Academy would go its separate way on a certain date and from that point on would be financially responsible for itself. ","type":"text"},{"content":"But Biemiller disagrees.","type":"text"},{"content":"“Drexel’s proposal was an immediate disaffiliation with no Drexel funding,” she said. “An immediate cessation of funding would have essentially put the Academy out of business. Any separation from Drexel which saves the Academy as an institution must be gradual.”","type":"text"},{"content":"She also objected to the characterization that the Academy’s proposal was inflammatory. Instead, she said, it was a “thoughtful, staged disaffiliation” that would have cost Drexel less than if it had moved forward with the terms for merger.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Who controls the Academy?","type":"header"},{"content":"The 2011 affiliation agreement that joined Drexel and the Academy does not address any commitment to fund the Academy if the parties disaffiliate. Drexel therefore would not be required to do so, according to Laura Solomon, founder of Laura Solomon & Associates, a law firm that exclusively represents charitable and other tax-exempt organizations and philanthropists. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“The parties could negotiate a ‘divorce’ in which Drexel had some kind of financial commitment (e.g., alimony) to support the sustainability of the Academy — but that would seem to be a tough ask at a time when educational institutions are facing their own financial challenges,” she said in an email.","type":"text"},{"content":"“While we understand the economic pressures that colleges and universities are facing today,” Biemiller said, “as a fiduciary board, it is our responsibility to work toward a solution that is in the best interests of the Academy and the people of Philadelphia and the scientists around the world who care about it.”","type":"text"},{"content":"Drexel currently has a lot of authority over the Academy under the 2011 agreement, with the right to approve its budget, choose its CEO and senior staff, and appoint its board. The Academy board can make recommendations, but the authority ultimately belongs to Drexel. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The Academy is a nonprofit corporation with a single member — Drexel. The Academy retains authority over its endowment, but delegated management of it to Drexel.","type":"text"},{"content":"But Drexel still was on the hook to cover the Academy’s deficits — as laid out in the affiliation agreement — noting it had provided $49 million in direct cash to the Academy over the last 15 years. A university representative told City Council last month that Drexel, which has been working to erase a deficit in its own budget, can no longer afford the $5 million to $6 million a year in support to the Academy. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Drexel, Merlo said, wanted the Academy to become a “wholly controlled subsidiary” of Drexel, which he said would have given the Drexel board more control over the Academy’s finances, yet maintained it as a separate nonprofit with its own assets and endowment.","type":"text"},{"content":"That means there would only be one fiduciary board — Drexel’s. ","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"It would have enabled Drexel’s board to deal with the Academy’s deficits, Merlo said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“You cannot have a subsidiary which is part of this bigger company that runs a $5 million deficit a year in perpetuity,” he said. “The new structure would have allowed [Drexel] to do the type of interventions you need.”","type":"text"},{"content":"But there were “guardrails” built in, Merlo said. Drexel, for example, would not have been able to dispose of assets of the Academy without a vote in favor by two-thirds of the Academy board.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"A solution in New Haven? ","type":"header"},{"content":"Just how long Drexel and the Academy will remain at an impasse is unclear. Academy board members serve three-year terms, which means as the terms of some expire, Drexel could replace them with new, like-minded board members.","type":"text"},{"content":"Merlo declined to comment on whether the university would take that step.","type":"text"},{"content":"“I would not like to speculate into the future,” he said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Cohen said he still thinks an agreement can be struck. Maybe it would take “some push from the governor and the mayor to get people back to the table,” he said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Merlo said he is hopeful the foundation-funded review will lead to solutions, similar to what happened with Yale University’s Peabody Museum, a natural history museum in New Haven, Conn. A donor gave $160 million, which galvanized others to donate. The museum closed for four years for renovations and reopened in 2024 offering free admission, with its attendance boosted several times over.","type":"text"},{"content":"On this, Merlo appears to be in complete agreement with a Save the Academy Coalition representative, who also mentioned the Peabody as a potential model for Philadelphia at the City Council hearing last month.","type":"text"},{"content":"“If they could do it in New Haven,” Merlo said, “I bet we could do it in Philadelphia.” ","type":"text"}],"credits":{"by":[{"_id":"snyder_susan","description":"I cover issues and trends affecting colleges. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Christopher Y. Shin from Cherry Hill, N.J., and Mary I. Cipperman of Devon, Pa., were among the 32 American students selected from a pool of more than 1,000 nominated by their colleges and universities for the full-ride scholarship to Oxford University. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Shin is a senior at Harvard<b> </b>University double majoring in chemical and physical biology and government. Cipperman graduated from Harvard in the spring with a bachelor’s in physics and a master’s in applied physics.","type":"text"},{"content":"During Shin’s time at Harvard he<b> </b>has researched infectious disease epidemiology with mathematical modeling and viral genomics to understand how to contain disease outbreaks. He also volunteers at Massachusetts General Hospital. Outside of science, math and medicine, he participates in the Harvard Model Congress and plays piano and trumpet. He plays in the Harvard Jazz Orchestra, is the former president of the Harvard Piano Society, and performs in a pop/funk student band.","type":"text"},{"content":"Once Shin arrives at Oxford next fall, he’ll pursue a master’s in modeling for global health and a master’s in genomic medicine. He said he hopes to become an administrator at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention someday and a physician scientist before that. The combination of biology and sociology embedded in the study of infectious disease first piqued his interest while studying at Harvard.","type":"text"},{"content":"He’s interested in “in how we as a society can better prepare, mitigate and prevent pandemics from occurring,” said Shin, 21, who attended Cherry Hill High School East. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“An ideal career trajectory I think for me would be anticipating threats like SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19 before they actually come to fruition and in the case we discover a COVID outbreak being able to respond with global partnership and governance,” he said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Cipperman currently researches applications of AI for clinical trial emulation and patient diagnosis as an Alex G. Booth fellow at the Mahmood Lab at Harvard. She also volunteers with hospice patients<b> </b>in the Cambridge area, was the president of the Harvard-Radcliffe Society of Physics Students, and has conducted research at CERN, the European laboratory for particle physics, to improve collision detection. ","type":"text"},{"content":"At Oxford, Cipperman will pursue a master’s in applied digital health and a master’s in medical physics with radiobiology. She aspires to ultimately become a physician scientist, she said, possibly specializing in oncology as a cancer survivor herself. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“I’m hoping to bridge clinical medicine with the advancements in science and technology that we’ve seen, especially in AI, over the past couple of years,” said Cipperman, 23, who attended Episcopal Academy in Newtown Square. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“A huge part of my academic plan is to actually not just develop AI but to develop also the auditing standards that ensure that it’s implemented in a way that’s ethical, safe and representative of various patients,” she said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Shin, Cipperman, and the 30 other Americans chosen for one of the academic world’s most elite awards will begin their studies at Oxford in October alongside scholars from 25 other regions from<b> </b>across the world. They will be part of an international cohort of<b> </b>around 100 scholars.","type":"text"},{"content":"More than 3,000 students started the application process and 1,006 of them were formally endorsed by more than 281 schools. ","type":"text"},{"content":"In addition to Shin and Cipperman from the U.S. cohort, two international University of Pennsylvania fourth-years were also awarded Rhodes scholarships: Lena Alshanafey, from Saudi Arabia, and Elliot Ross-Dick, from Trinidad and Tobago.","type":"text"},{"content":"Alshanafey is pursuing a dual degree in economics and political science in the Wharton School and the College of Arts and Sciences, with concentrations in finance and healthcare management. She’s a Joseph Wharton scholar through the Benjamin Franklin scholarship program, which aims to help foster students’ multidisciplinary interests. Her honors thesis uses hospital records to look at<b> </b>access to treatment for menopausal women in Saudi Arabia. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Alshanafey  also conducts research in Penn’s Department of Health Care Management and has led consulting projects for healthcare companies and startups. She has worked at Boston Consulting Group and Sanabil Investments, the venture arm of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, founded Novus Digest, a youth-led publication, and written for Arab News.","type":"text"},{"content":"At Oxford, Alshanafey will pursue master’s degrees in global health science and epidemiology and in applied digital health. She plans to return to Saudi Arabia to work in health policy and healthcare investing, using population-level evidence to identify gaps in women’s healthcare and guide investments toward models of care that reach women earlier.","type":"text"},{"content":"Ross-Dick is pursuing a mathematics degree in the college, with a minor in theatre arts. He is enrolled in the accelerated master’s program in International Educational Development and Research in the Graduate School of Education. He is a Penn World Scholar, a member of the Friars Senior Society, the Kinoki Senior Society, cast director for Mask and Wig, and a board member of Quadramics Theatre Company.","type":"text"},{"content":"At Oxford, Ross-Dick plans to pursue master’s degrees in education research design and methodology and comparative and international education. He will research the application of a culturally relevant framework to Caribbean education as a means of decolonizing the region’s education system.","type":"text"}],"credits":{"by":[{"_id":"munro_dana","description":"I cover breaking news and write general assignment stories. inno-p--has-dropcap\">It’s a brand-new year for The 76, The Inquirer’s annual list of the most vital restaurants in the Philadelphia area. This year, we started fresh with a new batch of dining scouts and an even wider purview, diving deeper into pockets of Philadelphia that we didn’t get to eat through last year. The result is a list that we hope is as vibrant, diverse, and interesting as the city that it reflects.</p><p class=\"inno-p \">You’ll find some favorites from <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/food/inq2/best-restaurants-philadelphia-2024-20241015.html\">last year</a> on 2025’s 76, which held on to their spots by being just as impressive as they were the last times we ate there (<a href=\"#friday-saturday-sunday\">Friday Saturday Sunday</a> still dazzles, as does <a href=\"#gabriellas-vietnam\">Gabriella’s Vietnam</a>).</p><p class=\"inno-p \">But you’ll notice that there’s a good deal of turnover, too. More than half of the list is fresh — either classics we felt deserved their time in the spotlight, like the white-tablecloth red-gravy stalwart Dante & Luigi’s or chef favorite <a href=\"#pho-75\">Pho 75</a>, or new and new-to-us spots that reflect the shifting energy of the dining scene, like Indonesian karaoke hot spot <a href=\"http://niki-echo-cafe\">Niki Echo</a> and the revived <a href=\"#tequilas--la-jefa\">Tequilas</a>, a three-restaurants-in-one experience.</p><div class=\"inno-ad inno-layout--isolate inno-layout--align-full js-ad\"><div class=\"inno-ad__label\">Advertisement</div><div class=\"inno-ad__ad  inno-no-reset\"><div class=\"inline-ad\"></div></div></div><p class=\"inno-p \">Our scouts, all 18 of them, fanned out across the Philadelphia area and ate through cuisines we were curious about, like the wide-ranging food truck landscape and the vibrant Mexican community in Norristown. We found a Main Line cheesesteak (<a href=\"#johnnys-pizza\">Johnny’s Pizzeria</a>) that rivals South Philly’s best. The result is a list filled with gems, some in plain sight and some that required a bit more hunting.</p><p class=\"inno-p \">We think this list, which is unranked and alphabetical, is the most useful list of Philadelphia-area restaurants out there. Some hotly anticipated openings like Stephen Starr’s Borromini and Phila Lorn’s Sao opened too late to make the cut. But don’t worry, there’s always next year.</p><p class=\"inno-p \">The 76 is how we think Philadelphia is eating right now, and — we hope — might help you uncover your next favorite spot.
