— The nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening has highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure that has had several disruptive failures in recent months."},{"_id":"TKCGDRBHAFF3VL6UHVDK7AYQKY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Officials called the rare ground stop after outdated communications lines became overloaded and began to fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin."},{"_id":"FZOF62F64NGKLEH4ZJA2WSEY5Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The breakdown occurred less than two months after a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush International Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line."},{"_id":"KHKDJEBNPBEXRJ2IHKVQV2HNFY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the FAA has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. The FAA has yet to identify precisely what caused communication lines to falter."},{"_id":"JIGMDC7ICJEYBKHOIXOMNM5XIA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Associated Press reported that Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said Saturday that the U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of today. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”"},{"_id":"YNB7FWHTTNH4HCZI6C7VXIL2XQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said."},{"_id":"DFIKVJG35JEFJGLK45KPK2R74A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause."},{"_id":"QPKYH6LC3FG6NM6YFT3OFZA2PI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment,” Duffy said."},{"_id":"5NEDTLYXOZBLLNUDK2NKRHVJ7E","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the successive episodes of such problems have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that continue to hamper air traffic controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after concerted efforts to make improvements. And they raised questions about whether the federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems and redundancies to prevent disruptive or even catastrophic failures."},{"_id":"BNMOUXOZTJD3RP2MRJYRKHKNXM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"For decades, air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks, and alphabetical keyboards so old that the FAA has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to help pay for upgrades, after a series of outages in air traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, caused alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities."},{"_id":"LSZ4PGSALZDSBO7T45UN6CBGQY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecoms contractor tasked to manage the system upgrades, boasted on its website that it had converted about 70% of the copper line to fiber optic cable; last week, the FAA announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks."},{"_id":"Q6KS2XJEOFGV7FBDZETY33EUCI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the disruptions in recent weeks showed that those upgrades had serious vulnerabilities themselves."},{"_id":"E6BY4EP4HZBC5BTBVRQ2HDUTHQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered — to their surprise — had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later."},{"_id":"LSIQDWL3BZGHNFAPIYBN65E7AY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A similar incident occurred in October at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina, when a contractor working on plumbing accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. Just one day after that, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush International Airport, when yet another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line."},{"_id":"4Y5DCM5WBBFX7KO6TLENUQAHW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The fiber line upgrades themselves, Bedford, the FAA administrator, told reporters at the time, were not enough to save the system from failure."},{"_id":"ZQ54KCD6YZE4JPTQDGUFG2HSY4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Ideally, the FAA wanted to put data into cloud services, he told reporters then, so that “when you have a fiber cut, you have multiple pathways of backup.”"},{"_id":"FNIXXMAUH5A7BIE6SLYLM4ILQQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today we have physical fiber and when it’s cut, there’s one redundancy, and when we lose that, there’s no more redundancy,” he added."},{"_id":"LKQ6CSVCTZDJZL6OIZMOBBATOQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Friday’s national ground stop revealed that the lack of redundancies in the FAA’s system could trigger catastrophic failures in other ways and touched off a blame game in Washington. "},{"_id":"YIN3O24JS5H75C6P7CV4OWUFYQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy seized on the chaos to hammer Congress, saying it had failed to pony up enough funding to pay for systemwide upgrades."},{"_id":"LW5P2ARVM5FO5KM3WKHWZOSHCE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he told reporters at the White House Friday night, asking that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project. Their lack of action, he said, had forced his department to pursue patchwork upgrades that were insufficient. It was a dramatic increase in his demand for additional money, which for the past several months has hovered at $30 billion."},{"_id":"JKJJSB67KRFI7FIFUG2HT4LALI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But lawmakers in both parties are raising questions about how efficiently Duffy and the FAA have been spending the money they have already been given."},{"_id":"XVI7SMPNFVBE5LUJWUREJWIXOM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said in a statement issued shortly after Duffy’s news conference, accusing the administration of failing to take responsibility for its failures in “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents.”"},{"_id":"M435G3S22ZHQLHO2IYAZFDQKU4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in t</i><a href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/ground-stop-air-traffic-faa.html\"><i>he New York Times</i></a><i>.</i>"}],"copyright":"Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. Post"}},{"content_elements":[{"_id":"7PJC3WMHWJBS7G4SPGXECKU4XM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Sterban, a backup vocalist for Elvis Presley who went on to international acclaim as the bass singer for the Oak Ridge Boys, the country vocal quartet for whom he sang the “oom-papa-mow-mow” refrain on the 1981 blockbuster hit “Elvira,” died on Saturday in Hendersonville, Tenn. He was 83."},{"_id":"NK55NA2QMJE2DFRZUX43CO4GYM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His death was confirmed by his family and the Oak Ridge Boys. They said that Mr. Sterban, who had cancer, had died of complications from bronchitis and pneumonia."},{"_id":"D3ZYKRM6MBECRNOSI5GIMVWJKE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A singer of extraordinary range and power, Mr. Sterban could hit notes so low they could only be felt, as opposed to heard. He also could hit notes higher than many tenors can reach. His basso profundo not only anchored the Oak Ridge Boys’ gospel-steeped sound; it carried the occasional melodic lead on recordings like the group’s 1979 remake of the Righteous Brothers’ Top 40 pop hit “Dream On.”"},{"_id":"2QVF3XBHKJBYBGLXZMBQINVXZ4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His reverberating vocals galvanized the Oaks’ version of “Elvira,” a song that had previously been recorded by artists including Rodney Crowell and Kenny Rogers and the First Edition."},{"_id":"OPNCSNW3V5C25MOB5UXXZI5SQE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"It was never more than a minor hit, though, until Sterban’s stentorian “oom-papa-mow-mow” (framed by shouts of “Giddy up!” and “Hi-ho Silver!”) transformed it into a Grammy Award-winning record, and one of the most inescapable earworms of the early 1980s."},{"_id":"HRNHVASFUVHYXAYNDSADAZM6PM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“It absolutely carried us to another stratosphere,” Mr. Sterban explained in his 2012 memoir, <i>From Elvis to Elvira: My Life on Stage</i>, written with Steven Robinson. “The song, especially the lines I sang, was seemingly on everyone’s lips. It was unbelievable.”"},{"_id":"4JPJDLARYJFHHIGKNWUFWGMGBY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With 2 million copies sold, “Elvira” topped the country chart, crossing over to the pop Top 10 and helping secure the Oaks’ reputation as one of the most popular vocal groups in the history of country music."},{"_id":"XK7FPDGUUJCD5KU4YUHGMM4SVI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Besides Mr. Sterban, the group’s classic lineup, formed in the early 1970s, included lead singer Duane Allen; tenor Joe Bonsall, who died in 2024; and baritone William Lee Golden."},{"_id":"UHKRRJKLRRGVHICURYJLNXLT2M","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The group was formed as a gospel quartet in Oak Ridge, Tenn., in the early 1940s, disbanding and reforming at least twice before Mr. Sterban and Bonsall teamed up with Allen and Golden, stabilizing what had long been a mercurial lineup. Over the next two decades, the four men modernized the group’s original gospel sound with pop-country elements, placing 17 singles at the top of the country chart and 17 others in the country Top 10."},{"_id":"B2Q6R5HFGRF5LNYYCLFWGVZWSI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With records like “Elvira” and “Bobbie Sue” (1982), Mr. Sterban and the Oaks infused traditional country harmony singing with techniques popularized by R&B vocal groups like the Coasters and the Dominoes. They also contributed vocals to the likes of Paul Simon’s 1977 Top 10 pop hit “Slip Slidin’ Away.”"},{"_id":"7KC4MP27MVF3ZAQVVHXPEUR6PE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This more far-reaching aesthetic was hardly second nature to the group, though — at least, not at first."},{"_id":"ERLXZSXC5BC57HQ6BRNC5IEREI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This was especially the case when, at a commercial low point in the mid-’70s before they found a larger country audience, they went into the studio to sing backup on Jimmy Buffett’s “My Head Hurts, My Feet Stink, and I Don’t Love Jesus.”"},{"_id":"CHIMK35RHRADFCVFWFOHHY75VM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"35UGSUHYGNDZFIVT2IGUP7VLKA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“What in the world had we gotten ourselves into?” Mr. Sterban wrote in his memoir, describing how the members of the group felt at the time. They had already been accused of being sellouts by their core gospel following for performing covers of hits by the Eagles and Olivia Newton-John in concert."},{"_id":"TUGCD3VDNBES3FLJHF3DKH3ZWI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“All we could imagine,” he added, “were headlines confirming what many of our detractors already seemed to believe: ‘Oak Ridge Boys don’t love Jesus!’”"},{"_id":"NBQIM2TYHJFKNOVWFN6FEEOABQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"J4YY5RJBDNDADIB7JJ7AYHU55Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Anthony Sterban was born on April 24, 1943, in Camden, N.J., one of three children of Edward and Victoria (Giordano) Sterban. The son of Polish immigrants, his father was an electrician. His mother, a native of Salandra, a township in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, worked various jobs, including at a chocolate factory."},{"_id":"LPA2NXMT7NCHTJTNI2LCHATV2A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The product of a strict religious upbringing, young Richard began singing at the local Assembly of God church at 6 and went on to play tuba, sousaphone, and an assortment of other brass instruments in high school. While attending Trenton State College (now the College of New Jersey), he majored in music before dropping out to form the Keystone Quartet, a gospel group, in the early 1960s."},{"_id":"ZUO6CJEHWNBVPKDGNRHWWFSPUI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Life on the road, though, didn’t agree with some of the quartet’s members, and the group split up in early 1965, at which time Mr. Sterban took a job selling menswear at the Gimbels department store in northeast Philadelphia."},{"_id":"UEXL5CY5BBC53LAD7ENK662LHY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Shortly before that, he married Sandra Wilson, with whom he had three sons, Rich, Chris, and Doug."},{"_id":"OZ2KOW47O5GXNB756FJ2YXKU54","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In 1970, Mr. Sterban was hired to sing bass in the touring edition of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet, one of the premier Southern Gospel groups of the day."},{"_id":"4E4VGKSSFRFORM7EWVS6WWQJIQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A year later, the Stamps were hired to be Presley’s background singers, appearing with him at his four shows at Madison Square Garden in June 1972, as well as during his five-week residency in Las Vegas later that summer."},{"_id":"R342YOK6FNGUNEQHHYDO53QFV4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Mr. Sterban also sang on major recordings by Presley including “Burning Love,” a No. 2 pop hit in 1972, and “Always on My Mind.”"},{"_id":"5VCPEDP6DRAZRE4AGJHM7YFGBQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In October 1972, seizing the chance to be part of a headlining act of his own, Mr. Sterban accepted an invitation to join the Oak Ridge Boys, replacing bass singer Noel Fox."},{"_id":"HIAJ2BYFEZHRJEFNENKJAAFXPE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The newly reconstituted quartet initially struggled to make it in the country market. Buoyed, though, by a stint as regulars in Johnny Cash’s touring revue, they finally broke through to a wider audience with “Y’all Come Back Saloon.” A Top 10 country single in 1977, the record inaugurated a decade-plus string of hits that paved the way for sold-out concert tours, regular appearances on late-night television shows, and five Grammy Awards."},{"_id":"RXORM4FKIBEBJACWZ4L5CFH5HM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Oak Ridge Boys were inducted into the Gospel Hall of Fame in 2000 and into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015."},{"_id":"LI3YAWLWRVFB3DIJJAY57GSGZM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"An avid sports fan, Mr. Sterban was for years a part owner of — and occasional color commentator for — the Nashville Sounds baseball team, the Triple-A minor league affiliate of the Milwaukee Brewers. He also did color commentary for Vanderbilt University’s men’s baseball team."},{"_id":"KO7DW2YO2RCBHOZ66NNPOKUBNQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In addition to his sons from his first marriage, which ended in divorce, Mr. Sterban is survived by his second wife, Donna (Summers) Sterban; their daughters, Tori and Lauren; and several grandchildren."},{"_id":"RYQX5HPVEZHSHPN247LHATDMLE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"FYXJS5SOUFAPHDJHDO7JFO5DW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Their early struggles to find their stylistic equilibrium notwithstanding, the Oak Ridge Boys nevertheless continued to push the boundaries of country music decades after they found success with a more wide-ranging approach."},{"_id":"HLQ4WV4ILNDJHE4E3CUTRUSVEE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Maybe nowhere was this more evident than in their haunting 2009 rendition of the White Stripes’ 2003 single “Seven Nation Army.” Recorded with producer Dave Cobb, whose clients include Jason Isbell and Lady Gaga, the collaboration has been likened to Cash’s partnership with iconoclastic producer Rick Rubin."},{"_id":"IAI4HW7Q5RB5LES6KHYRB52JPY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“I think Dave took us down some roads we might not have traveled on our own,” Mr. Sterban was quoted as saying about the experience on the group’s website. “The music may be different, but he did not try to change us; he challenged us.”"},{"_id":"YB6JGHDCKFFPLCDB25PPHTEIKU","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in </i><a — The nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening has highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure that has had several disruptive failures in recent months."},{"_id":"TKCGDRBHAFF3VL6UHVDK7AYQKY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Officials called the rare ground stop after outdated communications lines became overloaded and began to fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin."},{"_id":"FZOF62F64NGKLEH4ZJA2WSEY5Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The breakdown occurred less than two months after a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush International Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line."},{"_id":"KHKDJEBNPBEXRJ2IHKVQV2HNFY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the FAA has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. The FAA has yet to identify precisely what caused communication lines to falter."},{"_id":"JIGMDC7ICJEYBKHOIXOMNM5XIA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Associated Press reported that Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said Saturday that the U.S. air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of today. He said airlines “will still have delays and cancellations” Saturday but promised that the “worst is behind us.”"},{"_id":"YNB7FWHTTNH4HCZI6C7VXIL2XQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours Friday, Trump administration officials said."},{"_id":"DFIKVJG35JEFJGLK45KPK2R74A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy said a contractor had been working on replacing a section of the system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire, and that work somehow caused the system overload. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor “incompetence” or a faulty router was the cause."},{"_id":"QPKYH6LC3FG6NM6YFT3OFZA2PI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment,” Duffy said."},{"_id":"5NEDTLYXOZBLLNUDK2NKRHVJ7E","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the successive episodes of such problems have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that continue to hamper air traffic controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after concerted efforts to make improvements. And they raised questions about whether the federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems and redundancies to prevent disruptive or even catastrophic failures."},{"_id":"BNMOUXOZTJD3RP2MRJYRKHKNXM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"For decades, air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks, and alphabetical keyboards so old that the FAA has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to help pay for upgrades, after a series of outages in air traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, caused alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities."},{"_id":"LSZ4PGSALZDSBO7T45UN6CBGQY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecoms contractor tasked to manage the system upgrades, boasted on its website that it had converted about 70% of the copper line to fiber optic cable; last week, the FAA announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks."},{"_id":"Q6KS2XJEOFGV7FBDZETY33EUCI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But the disruptions in recent weeks showed that those upgrades had serious vulnerabilities themselves."},{"_id":"E6BY4EP4HZBC5BTBVRQ2HDUTHQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered — to their surprise — had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later."},{"_id":"LSIQDWL3BZGHNFAPIYBN65E7AY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A similar incident occurred in October at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina, when a contractor working on plumbing accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. Just one day after that, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush International Airport, when yet another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line."},{"_id":"4Y5DCM5WBBFX7KO6TLENUQAHW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The fiber line upgrades themselves, Bedford, the FAA administrator, told reporters at the time, were not enough to save the system from failure."},{"_id":"ZQ54KCD6YZE4JPTQDGUFG2HSY4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Ideally, the FAA wanted to put data into cloud services, he told reporters then, so that “when you have a fiber cut, you have multiple pathways of backup.”"},{"_id":"FNIXXMAUH5A7BIE6SLYLM4ILQQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today we have physical fiber and when it’s cut, there’s one redundancy, and when we lose that, there’s no more redundancy,” he added."},{"_id":"LKQ6CSVCTZDJZL6OIZMOBBATOQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Friday’s national ground stop revealed that the lack of redundancies in the FAA’s system could trigger catastrophic failures in other ways and touched off a blame game in Washington. "},{"_id":"YIN3O24JS5H75C6P7CV4OWUFYQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Duffy seized on the chaos to hammer Congress, saying it had failed to pony up enough funding to pay for systemwide upgrades."},{"_id":"LW5P2ARVM5FO5KM3WKHWZOSHCE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he told reporters at the White House Friday night, asking that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project. Their lack of action, he said, had forced his department to pursue patchwork upgrades that were insufficient. It was a dramatic increase in his demand for additional money, which for the past several months has hovered at $30 billion."},{"_id":"JKJJSB67KRFI7FIFUG2HT4LALI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"But lawmakers in both parties are raising questions about how efficiently Duffy and the FAA have been spending the money they have already been given."},{"_id":"XVI7SMPNFVBE5LUJWUREJWIXOM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said in a statement issued shortly after Duffy’s news conference, accusing the administration of failing to take responsibility for its failures in “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents.”"},{"_id":"M435G3S22ZHQLHO2IYAZFDQKU4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in t</i><a href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/ground-stop-air-traffic-faa.html\"><i>he New York Times</i></a><i>.</i>"}],"copyright":"Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. Post"}},{"content_elements":[{"_id":"7PJC3WMHWJBS7G4SPGXECKU4XM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Sterban, a backup vocalist for Elvis Presley who went on to international acclaim as the bass singer for the Oak Ridge Boys, the country vocal quartet for whom he sang the “oom-papa-mow-mow” refrain on the 1981 blockbuster hit “Elvira,” died on Saturday in Hendersonville, Tenn. He was 83."},{"_id":"NK55NA2QMJE2DFRZUX43CO4GYM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His death was confirmed by his family and the Oak Ridge Boys. They said that Mr. Sterban, who had cancer, had died of complications from bronchitis and pneumonia."},{"_id":"D3ZYKRM6MBECRNOSI5GIMVWJKE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A singer of extraordinary range and power, Mr. Sterban could hit notes so low they could only be felt, as opposed to heard. He also could hit notes higher than many tenors can reach. His basso profundo not only anchored the Oak Ridge Boys’ gospel-steeped sound; it carried the occasional melodic lead on recordings like the group’s 1979 remake of the Righteous Brothers’ Top 40 pop hit “Dream On.”"},{"_id":"2QVF3XBHKJBYBGLXZMBQINVXZ4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"His reverberating vocals galvanized the Oaks’ version of “Elvira,” a song that had previously been recorded by artists including Rodney Crowell and Kenny Rogers and the First Edition."},{"_id":"OPNCSNW3V5C25MOB5UXXZI5SQE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"It was never more than a minor hit, though, until Sterban’s stentorian “oom-papa-mow-mow” (framed by shouts of “Giddy up!” and “Hi-ho Silver!”) transformed it into a Grammy Award-winning record, and one of the most inescapable earworms of the early 1980s."},{"_id":"HRNHVASFUVHYXAYNDSADAZM6PM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“It absolutely carried us to another stratosphere,” Mr. Sterban explained in his 2012 memoir, <i>From Elvis to Elvira: My Life on Stage</i>, written with Steven Robinson. “The song, especially the lines I sang, was seemingly on everyone’s lips. It was unbelievable.”"},{"_id":"4JPJDLARYJFHHIGKNWUFWGMGBY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With 2 million copies sold, “Elvira” topped the country chart, crossing over to the pop Top 10 and helping secure the Oaks’ reputation as one of the most popular vocal groups in the history of country music."},{"_id":"XK7FPDGUUJCD5KU4YUHGMM4SVI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Besides Mr. Sterban, the group’s classic lineup, formed in the early 1970s, included lead singer Duane Allen; tenor Joe Bonsall, who died in 2024; and baritone William Lee Golden."},{"_id":"UHKRRJKLRRGVHICURYJLNXLT2M","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The group was formed as a gospel quartet in Oak Ridge, Tenn., in the early 1940s, disbanding and reforming at least twice before Mr. Sterban and Bonsall teamed up with Allen and Golden, stabilizing what had long been a mercurial lineup. Over the next two decades, the four men modernized the group’s original gospel sound with pop-country elements, placing 17 singles at the top of the country chart and 17 others in the country Top 10."},{"_id":"B2Q6R5HFGRF5LNYYCLFWGVZWSI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"With records like “Elvira” and “Bobbie Sue” (1982), Mr. Sterban and the Oaks infused traditional country harmony singing with techniques popularized by R&B vocal groups like the Coasters and the Dominoes. They also contributed vocals to the likes of Paul Simon’s 1977 Top 10 pop hit “Slip Slidin’ Away.”"},{"_id":"7KC4MP27MVF3ZAQVVHXPEUR6PE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This more far-reaching aesthetic was hardly second nature to the group, though — at least, not at first."},{"_id":"ERLXZSXC5BC57HQ6BRNC5IEREI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This was especially the case when, at a commercial low point in the mid-’70s before they found a larger country audience, they went into the studio to sing backup on Jimmy Buffett’s “My Head Hurts, My Feet Stink, and I Don’t Love Jesus.”"},{"_id":"CHIMK35RHRADFCVFWFOHHY75VM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"35UGSUHYGNDZFIVT2IGUP7VLKA","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“What in the world had we gotten ourselves into?” Mr. Sterban wrote in his memoir, describing how the members of the group felt at the time. They had already been accused of being sellouts by their core gospel following for performing covers of hits by the Eagles and Olivia Newton-John in concert."},{"_id":"TUGCD3VDNBES3FLJHF3DKH3ZWI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“All we could imagine,” he added, “were headlines confirming what many of our detractors already seemed to believe: ‘Oak Ridge Boys don’t love Jesus!’”"},{"_id":"NBQIM2TYHJFKNOVWFN6FEEOABQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"J4YY5RJBDNDADIB7JJ7AYHU55Y","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Richard Anthony Sterban was born on April 24, 1943, in Camden, N.J., one of three children of Edward and Victoria (Giordano) Sterban. The son of Polish immigrants, his father was an electrician. His mother, a native of Salandra, a township in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, worked various jobs, including at a chocolate factory."},{"_id":"LPA2NXMT7NCHTJTNI2LCHATV2A","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The product of a strict religious upbringing, young Richard began singing at the local Assembly of God church at 6 and went on to play tuba, sousaphone, and an assortment of other brass instruments in high school. While attending Trenton State College (now the College of New Jersey), he majored in music before dropping out to form the Keystone Quartet, a gospel group, in the early 1960s."},{"_id":"ZUO6CJEHWNBVPKDGNRHWWFSPUI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Life on the road, though, didn’t agree with some of the quartet’s members, and the group split up in early 1965, at which time Mr. Sterban took a job selling menswear at the Gimbels department store in northeast Philadelphia."},{"_id":"UEXL5CY5BBC53LAD7ENK662LHY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Shortly before that, he married Sandra Wilson, with whom he had three sons, Rich, Chris, and Doug."},{"_id":"OZ2KOW47O5GXNB756FJ2YXKU54","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In 1970, Mr. Sterban was hired to sing bass in the touring edition of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet, one of the premier Southern Gospel groups of the day."},{"_id":"4E4VGKSSFRFORM7EWVS6WWQJIQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A year later, the Stamps were hired to be Presley’s background singers, appearing with him at his four shows at Madison Square Garden in June 1972, as well as during his five-week residency in Las Vegas later that summer."},{"_id":"R342YOK6FNGUNEQHHYDO53QFV4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Mr. Sterban also sang on major recordings by Presley including “Burning Love,” a No. 2 pop hit in 1972, and “Always on My Mind.”"},{"_id":"5VCPEDP6DRAZRE4AGJHM7YFGBQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In October 1972, seizing the chance to be part of a headlining act of his own, Mr. Sterban accepted an invitation to join the Oak Ridge Boys, replacing bass singer Noel Fox."},{"_id":"HIAJ2BYFEZHRJEFNENKJAAFXPE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The newly reconstituted quartet initially struggled to make it in the country market. Buoyed, though, by a stint as regulars in Johnny Cash’s touring revue, they finally broke through to a wider audience with “Y’all Come Back Saloon.” A Top 10 country single in 1977, the record inaugurated a decade-plus string of hits that paved the way for sold-out concert tours, regular appearances on late-night television shows, and five Grammy Awards."},{"_id":"RXORM4FKIBEBJACWZ4L5CFH5HM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The Oak Ridge Boys were inducted into the Gospel Hall of Fame in 2000 and into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015."},{"_id":"LI3YAWLWRVFB3DIJJAY57GSGZM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"An avid sports fan, Mr. Sterban was for years a part owner of — and occasional color commentator for — the Nashville Sounds baseball team, the Triple-A minor league affiliate of the Milwaukee Brewers. He also did color commentary for Vanderbilt University’s men’s baseball team."},{"_id":"KO7DW2YO2RCBHOZ66NNPOKUBNQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In addition to his sons from his first marriage, which ended in divorce, Mr. Sterban is survived by his second wife, Donna (Summers) Sterban; their daughters, Tori and Lauren; and several grandchildren."},{"_id":"RYQX5HPVEZHSHPN247LHATDMLE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":""},{"_id":"FYXJS5SOUFAPHDJHDO7JFO5DW4","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Their early struggles to find their stylistic equilibrium notwithstanding, the Oak Ridge Boys nevertheless continued to push the boundaries of country music decades after they found success with a more wide-ranging approach."},{"_id":"HLQ4WV4ILNDJHE4E3CUTRUSVEE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Maybe nowhere was this more evident than in their haunting 2009 rendition of the White Stripes’ 2003 single “Seven Nation Army.” Recorded with producer Dave Cobb, whose clients include Jason Isbell and Lady Gaga, the collaboration has been likened to Cash’s partnership with iconoclastic producer Rick Rubin."},{"_id":"IAI4HW7Q5RB5LES6KHYRB52JPY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"“I think Dave took us down some roads we might not have traveled on our own,” Mr. Sterban was quoted as saying about the experience on the group’s website. “The music may be different, but he did not try to change us; he challenged us.”"},{"_id":"YB6JGHDCKFFPLCDB25PPHTEIKU","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"<i>This article originally appeared in </i><a
